session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Participants will be framed as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the specific places they go, the food they eat, the company they keep. The collective identity is 'men in the UK thinking about how they live day-to-day', not researchers or experts on masculinity. I will avoid framing them as people with opinions on gender theory and instead keep the anchor concrete: what they actually do, eat, and experience.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or defensively dismissive answers ('gender doesn't affect what I eat'). Will require behavioural grounding early — getting to specific moments and past events rather than general attitudes.

Social acceptability of plant-based foods (Sections 4–5): Risk of consensus hardening quickly around practical/cost barriers, masking deeper identity and social concerns. Will need sharpening moves and dissent invitations.

The relationship between masculine identity and food: Participants may hold implicit associations between meat and masculinity without being able to name them directly. Contradictions between stated positions and described behaviours are the most valuable data here — must track carefully.

What would actually need to change for plant-based eating to be viable (Section 4): Risk of abstract or aspirational answers. Need to keep this grounded in real constraints — social, practical, emotional — not just stated preferences.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Unknown from profile alone — 45, suburban South East. May be relatively comfortable in group settings given age and context, but no strong prior anticipation.

48, suburban East of England. Oldest of the group by a small margin. May be more settled in his views; could either anchor the group or resist novelty. Worth watching for early opinion-leadership signals.

45, suburban South West. No distinguishing profile markers. Monitor for early reticence — South West context sometimes associated with more traditional attitudes that could feel less speakable in a group.

40, suburban North West. Youngest of the group by 5 years. May hold somewhat different reference points from the others. Worth tracking whether he self-positions as different from the older participants.
47, suburban South East — same region as Andrew. Possible rapport between them if they pick up on that. No other distinguishing markers.

known_risk_conditions: Topic produces socially desirable answers by design — men discussing gender and food choices are likely to present themselves as more flexible or enlightened than their actual behaviour. Behavioural grounding (specific past events, real meals, named occasions) is essential from Section 2 onward.

Consensus risk is structurally high in an all-male group on a topic that touches masculine identity — participants may align around a shared 'laddish pragmatism' frame that masks real diversity. Must watch for premature convergence, especially in Sections 3–5.

The word 'gender' (Section 3 scripted question) may trigger a defensive or intellectualised response. If participants pivot to abstract gender-theory language or blanket dismissal ('no, I just eat what I fancy'), will need a quick behavioural redirect without leading.

Plant-based eating carries active stigma in some male social contexts — participants may perform indifference or mild hostility for social reasons rather than expressing genuine attitudes. Indirect probing (social context, what others think, specific scenarios) will be more useful than direct attitude questions.
Group is entirely suburban UK men in their 40s — high homogeneity increases conformity risk. Need to work harder to surface genuine diversity of experience than with a mixed-profile group.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro, opening context): Very light touch. The goal is rapport and getting voices in the room. Minimal probing — enough to hear from everyone, not enough to exhaust the warmup topics. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): Moderate directivity. Begin transitioning from general attitudes to specific behaviours. Introduce behavioural grounding here so the norm is established before we hit the sensitive sections. Sections 3–5 (main topics): Highest directivity. Active use of contradictions, dissent invitations, and behavioural probes. Do not let abstract answers stand unchallenged. Use sharpening moves when consensus forms too quickly. Section 6 (closing): Very light. Offer space for addition but do not reopen closed topics or probe for depth.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the core research weight and receive the largest share combined (~55% of total budget). Context sections (1, 2) serve as warm-up and behavioural grounding and receive a moderate share (~30%). Intro and closing are functional bookends and receive minimal budget (~15% combined).

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?
